items.stem: Felix writes: "If f(x) = kx on [0, 2] then k = 1/2 because f(2) must be 1." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: ∫₀² kx dx = 2k = 1, so k = 1/2 here, but the reason is total area 1, not f(2) = 1.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the number of sixes in 10 rolls of a fair die is binomial.
items.answer: There are 10 independent trials, each giving six or not six, with constant probability 1/6.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: There are 10 independent trials, each giving six or not six, with constant probability 1/6. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Aiko scored 69 in History (mean 63, s.d. 10) and 73 in Biology (mean 65, s.d. 8). Both are normally distributed. Explain, using z-scores, in which subject the performance was relatively better.
items.markingKey: z = 0.600 for History (A1); z = 1.00 for Biology (A1); larger z is better relative to the cohort (R1).

items.stem: Explain why the table X = 1, 2, 3 with P(X = x) = 0.3, 0.4, 0.4 cannot be a probability distribution.
items.markingKey: Σ P(X = x) = 1.1 (A1); a probability distribution must sum to 1 (R1); so the table is invalid (R1).

items.stem: Noah says that if Var(X) = 6 then Var(3X − 4) = 14. Explain the error and give the correct value.
items.markingKey: subtracting 4 shifts all values and does not change spread (R1); multiplying by 3 multiplies deviations by 3, so the variance by 9 (R1); 54 (A1).

items.stem: "P(X < 3) = P(X ≤ 3) for a binomial variable." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.markingKey: X is discrete: P(X < 3) = P(X ≤ 2). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.
